sections.h2: Where is Jefferson County and which offices handle its property tax?
sections.html:
Jefferson County is in southern Illinois, in the area locals call Little Egypt, and Mt. Vernon is the county seat. The county was organized on March 26, 1819, and covers 571 square miles of land. Interstates 57 and 64 and U.S. 51 run through it, and its western edge touches the St. Louis commuter region.

Two courthouse offices matter most to a seller. The Treasurer/Collector sits at 100 South 10th Street, Room 100, Mt. Vernon, and answers at 618-244-8010 and keeps weekday hours that end at 4 p.m. The Assessor, whose formal title is Supervisor of Assessments, is in the same building at 618-244-8016. The Assessor also acts as clerk of the Board of Review, so appeals and exemption forms both run through that desk.

The treasurer's page is blunt about what it cannot do. Use this split before you call:

  • Mailing address changes on a bill, and every homestead, disability or senior freeze exemption: Assessor.
  • Complaints about how large the bill is: the taxing districts listed on the bill itself.
  • Redemption of delinquent tax: County Clerk, 618-244-8020.
  • Paying or asking about a payment: Treasurer/Collector.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about owning a home in Jefferson County?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts counts 36,147 residents for July 2025, about 2.6 percent fewer than at the 2020 count. Of the 14,820 households, 71.7 percent own their home, and the typical owner-occupied house was valued at $126,000 across the 2020 to 2024 survey years. Households earned a median $63,118 in that stretch.

Against a house worth $126,000, a delinquent bill or a roof repair can take a real share of a seller's equity. Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,278, and owners without one report $578. If your tax bill is behind and you want to skip listing prep, an as-is sale to a cash buyer is a route to weigh against a traditional listing.

sections.h2: How does Jefferson County bill and collect real estate tax?
sections.html:
The county bills a year behind and posts a calendar on its Treasurer page. Tax for the 2025 assessment year is payable in 2026, and the statute lets an installment go delinquent after the later of June 1 or the due date printed on the bill, then charges 1 1/2 percent per month or part of a month in a county this size (35 ILCS 200/21-15). A payment postmarked on or before the due date is on time.

Jefferson County dates for 2025 real estate tax payable in 2026 (source: Jefferson County Treasurer/Collector)
EventDate on the county page
Bills mailedJuly 29, 2026
First installment dueAugust 28, 2026
Second installment dueSeptember 28, 2026
Delinquent tax publishedNovember 5, 2026
Annual tax sale auctionNovember 20, 2026

Mobile home tax runs on its own track: the page lists May 22, 2026 as that year's due date. The dates move from one cycle to the next, so request the calendar for whichever year your closing falls in.

sections.h2: How can I pay Jefferson County property tax?
sections.html:
The county accepts payment several ways, and each has its own condition. Checks go to the Jefferson County Collector.

  • Online by scanning the QR code on the bill. E-checks carry no fee, and cards carry a charge printed as 2.25% or a $2.00 minimum.
  • Most local banks, only up to the due date. Banks refuse late payments, and the stub must come with you.
  • U.S. Mail, postmarked no later than the installment date, with the stub.
  • In person at the courthouse office, where only cash, checks and money orders are taken.

The page adds that a personal check should reach the office 45 or more days before the tax sale so the bank has time to process it. If a mortgage company pays from escrow, you are the one who must forward the bill to them. Owners who want a bill that never arrives late can enroll in paperless billing or autopay through the county's online payment site.

The county also runs an optional prepayment plan. From the first business day of the month after the second installment is due, about six months of prepayments toward the next bill are accepted, up to 100 percent of the last bill, provided all prior taxes are current.

sections.h2: What changed about the Jefferson County tax sale?
sections.html:
Two recent changes affect anyone with unpaid tax. The Treasurer's tax auction page says that, starting with the 2025 tax payable in 2026, the county elected under Public Act 104-0553 to acquire delinquent real estate taxes itself as trustee for the taxing districts. It also says the county adopted the Single Bidder Rule effective January 2026. Delinquent mobile home taxes still go to private tax buyers.

A separate sealed bid auction offers properties foreclosed for unpaid real estate tax, and bids may be placed online through iltaxsale.com. Under state law, property sold at a tax sale can generally be redeemed within 3 years of the sale date, with exceptions tied to the property's condition on that date (35 ILCS 200/21-350). Redemption goes through the County Clerk.

Mobile homes have an extra step. Taxes must be paid up to date before the home is moved or sold, and a tax certification from the Treasurer's office, costing $5, is filed with the Illinois Secretary of State to clear the title. Unpaid mobile home tax from earlier years must be settled before the county takes current-year payment.

sections.h2: What is the route for challenging a Jefferson County assessment?
sections.html:
File a written complaint with the Board of Review, which the Assessor's office administers. The county page listed April 6, 2026 as the deadline for 2025 assessments, and that window has closed. State law sets the general clock at 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55), so watch the newspaper notice each year.

Three appointed members sit on the Board of Review. If you disagree with its written decision, the Property Tax Appeal Board takes appeals filed within 30 days of that notice (35 ILCS 200/16-160). Assessments outside Cook County are set at 33 1/3 percent of fair cash value (35 ILCS 200/9-155), and the published notice gives a median level you can use to test your own figure.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can a Jefferson County homeowner use?
sections.html:
The Assessor's exemption page lists the common homestead reductions. The dollar amounts below are as the county prints them, and each reduces equalized assessed value rather than the bill directly.

  • General homestead: the rise in value since 1977, up to $6,000, for an owner who lives in the home.
  • Senior citizen homestead: $5,000 for owners 65 or older.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income of $65,000 or less for the 2025 application, with a new state law raising the limit in later years.
  • Homestead improvement: up to $75,000 of added value per year, for four years after the work is done.
  • Persons with disabilities: $2,000. Returning veterans: $5,000 for two years.
  • Veterans with disabilities: $2,500 at 30 to under 50 percent, $5,000 at 50 to under 70 percent, and the first $250,000 of value at 70 percent or more.

The senior deferral program works like a loan. It allows up to $7,500 of tax per year to be deferred at 3 percent simple interest, with the amount due when the home is sold or on death. Applications run from January 1 through March 1. A seller on this program should request a payoff figure from the Treasurer before listing.

sections.h2: What should a Jefferson County seller handle before closing?
sections.html:
Start with a printout from the county's property tax inquiry site, jeffersonil.devnetwedge.com, which shows bills and payments by parcel. Give your title company the parcel number and the mailing address on record. If you moved out, file a change of address with the Assessor so the next bill reaches the new owner or the lender.

Next, confirm whether any installment is unpaid, whether a deferral lien exists, and whether the home is on a mortgage escrow. Have your title company explain how the year's tax will be divided at closing, and put in the contract who pays the bill that arrives afterward. If a bill is already delinquent, get the interest-inclusive figure from the Treasurer, and ask the County Clerk about any sold tax.

faqs.q: What dates appear on a Jefferson County tax calendar?
faqs.a: The county calendar for taxes payable in 2026 lists August 28 and September 28 as the two installment dates. The date printed on your bill controls, and the calendar changes by year, so request the cycle that matches your closing.

faqs.q: Who handles exemptions in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: The Assessor's office, at 618-244-8016. The Treasurer states that it cannot help with homestead, disability or senior freeze exemptions or with address changes on bills.

faqs.q: Can I pay Jefferson County tax with a card?
faqs.a: Yes, online, and the county page prints a fee of 2.25% or a $2.00 minimum. E-checks have no fee, and the courthouse counter takes only cash, checks and money orders.

faqs.q: What happens if Jefferson County tax stays unpaid?
faqs.a: The installment accrues interest after the due date, the parcel is published as delinquent, and the amount goes to the annual tax sale. Redemption after a sale is handled by the County Clerk at 618-244-8020.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay tax before selling a mobile home in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer says mobile home taxes must be paid to date before a move or sale, and a $5 tax certification is needed for a clear title through the Illinois Secretary of State.
